exampleAnswers.Purpose and audience: A product demonstration narrative with realistic steps, success checks, and fallback notes.
exampleAnswers.Working context: This fictional demonstration follows an owner preparing a project handover with an Agent. The narrative is illustrative and should be aligned with the actual product’s verified capabilities before presentation.
exampleAnswers.Example records:
Step: 1 · What the audience sees: A short project brief · Point to explain: The owner supplies the goal
Step: 2 · What the audience sees: A draft document index · Point to explain: The Agent prepares a reviewable result
Step: 3 · What the audience sees: The owner reviews a detail · Point to explain: Decisions stay visible
Step: 4 · What the audience sees: A finished handover · Point to explain: The next person has a clear starting point
exampleAnswers.Content decisions:
Begin with a real task: Introduce the person, the project, and the difficulty in one minute. Avoid opening with a tour of every navigation item. The audience needs a reason to care about the next action.
Demonstrate the boundary: Show the draft and the owner’s review as separate moments. Use only capabilities that exist in the version being demonstrated, and identify sample data clearly.
Keep a fallback: Prepare screenshots of the same example in case the live environment is unavailable. Explain that the fallback is a recorded illustration rather than pretending the product is responding live.
exampleAnswers.Format and interaction: deck layout; section navigation and expandable detail where useful; matching landscape presentation PDF.
exampleAnswers.Sharing and provenance: A hypothetical example informed by Claw Me’s small-team and Agent workflows. These are not Pete’s actual clients, finances, travel plans, research results, or commitments. Keep the real adaptation private until the owner chooses to share.
